summary: This RFC discusses problems of connecting personal computers to the ARPA Internet over low-speed links and possible solutions. It is a discussion paper that says none of its proposals are meant as standards. It is historic.

eli5.summary: Home computers with slow connections have trouble joining the big network. This note asks people to talk about how to help them.

questions: how to connect personal computers to the internet in 1984
how to compress tcp ip headers on slow links
subtitle: A 1984 discussion paper on squeezing TCP/IP over slow modem lines, with three proposed ways to do it.

tldr.problem: Personal computers dialing in over 1200 or 2400 baud modems waste most of the line on 41-byte TCP/IP packets, even for a single typed character.
tldr.mechanism: Three Thinwire schemes are proposed: Thinwire I sends only the changes from the previous packet, Thinwire II keeps a template per connection and sends compact updates, and Thinwire III lets a gateway handle TCP/IP for the PC over one multiplexed reliable stream.
tldr.outcome: None of the proposals are intended as standards. The RFC is a discussion paper, and its status is Historic.

today: RFC 914 is Historic, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. The text itself says none of its proposals are intended as standards for the ARPA-Internet.

sections.title: The Problem with Thin Wires
sections.content:
Workstations and personal computers costing $3 to 10K can be placed in homes and offices far from high-speed connections. Dedicated 56k baud lines are costly and slow to install, and fast LANs do not reach them, so 1200 and 2400 baud phone modems will be important. The paper calls a path under 9600 baud a thin data path.

A minimum TCP/IP Telnet packet carrying one character is 41 bytes. At 1200 baud that takes around 0.3 seconds, which is like using a 30 baud line for single-character transmission. The authors say real-world overhead could make times 10 to 50 percent worse. Local echo and line editing help, but many applications need character-at-a-time transmission, and multiple data streams are also useful.
sections.eli5: Mailing a one-letter note in a huge envelope on a slow road wastes nearly all the trip. The envelope is the problem, not the letter.

sections.title: Three Kinds of Solution
sections.content:
The RFC lists three forms a solution can take. The first is a non-solution: live with the slow link, which may be fine for background file transfer or one-time inquiries. The second is to intercept link-level transmissions and compress them, which gives a symmetric structure on both sides of the thin wire. The third is an asymmetric gateway that takes transport and network overhead away from both the serial link and the PC.

Compression yields two designs, Thinwire I and II. The gateway approach is Thinwire III. The RFC's estimates for single-character traffic are: 30 baud effective for plain TCP/IP on a 1200 baud line, about 70 for Thinwire I, 95 for Thinwire II, and around 900 for Thinwire III.
sections.eli5: You can put up with the slowness, shrink the envelopes, or hire a helper to deal with most of the paperwork.

sections.title: Thinwire I: Send Only the Changes
sections.content:
Both ends store the most recent packet and the sender transmits only what changed. An update is a series of descriptor and data blocks. Each descriptor is one byte with two four-bit fields, an offset from the last changed byte and a count of bytes to substitute, so offsets and counts up to 15 can be described. In the worst case the descriptor adds one byte per 15, about 6 percent expansion.

In the appendix example, two single-character Telnet packets are 41 bytes each, and the update for the second is 17 bytes. A descriptor with offset 0 and count 0 ends the update. The scheme is simple, but compression is modest and breaks down when several classes of packet share the link, because they no longer have common headers.
sections.eli5: Instead of re-sending the whole letter, you only say which words changed since the last one.

sections.title: Thinwire II: Templates per Connection
sections.content:
Thinwire II uses knowledge of the protocols. Packets are sorted into classes, such as one class per TCP connection, by matching templates on fields that do not change (network type, version, type of service, protocol, and source and destination addresses and ports). Only changed fields are sent, flagged by a bitfield, and simple arithmetic lets 32-bit fields be updated in 8 or 16 bits. The example reduces 41 bytes to 13 bytes.

The update header has an UPDATE bit, a LONG bit, a template number, a length and, for a new template, a type of packet (0 unknown, 1 TCP/IP, 2 UDP/IP). Costs include memory for many templates and the gateway keeping tables. Because both sides keep state, a loss of synchronization stops data flow, so the serial line must be reliable and there must be periodic resynchronization, such as sending every Nth packet in full. Unrecognized packet types are sent in full, and three zero-length, template 0, type 0 packets clear the template tables.
sections.eli5: Both sides keep a copy of each conversation's usual label, so after the first message they only say what is different.

sections.title: Thinwire III: A Gateway as Agent
sections.content:
Thinwire III is a star network with a gateway in the center. The PC does not run full transport and internet layers. Instead the PC and the gateway share one reliable serial stream (SLIP or equivalent) carrying data and control requests, and the gateway opens TCP, UDP and later TP4 connections on the PC's behalf. Inline logical switches pick the connection the data belongs to.

The scheme is not symmetric. The gateway cannot open inbound connections to the PC, which is treated as a stub host, but the PC may passively open connections on the gateway to act as a server. Flow control is mostly left to buffering and process blocking, with control messages for rare cases. The tentative specification uses the ASCII character z as an escape, with request codes in ranges for connection switching (0 to 31), stream opens (64 to 127), datagrams (128 to 191) and control requests (192 to 254), and code 255 for replies. The RFC marks it tentative, with unresolved issues such as scheduling of serial line use.
sections.eli5: The PC gives one note to a helper at the other end. The helper makes all the phone calls and does the paperwork for it.

sections.title: The SLIP Message Format
sections.content:
The appendix describes the Serial Line Interface Protocol (SLIP) as a reliable link beneath Thinwire. A message begins with a 1-byte Start of Header token (11111111), then a 4-bit sequence number (SEQ), a 4-bit acknowledgement number (ACK), a 5-bit length and 3 flag bits, followed by up to 32 bytes of data and an exclusive-or checksum byte.

The flags mark a receive error (LACK, meaning the ACK repeats the last acknowledged message), a Synchronize Sequence Numbers message (SSNM) and a Start of Control Message (SOCM). The sender may not go more than four messages past the last acknowledged one, a window of four. Startup uses a three-way handshake taken from TCP. Bad checksums trigger a LACK, and the receiver throws away out-of-order messages instead of resequencing them.
sections.eli5: Each little packet is numbered and checked, and if one is damaged the receiver says so and the sender repeats it.
